title: State Across Sessions
summary: Persistence resumes one conversation; cross-session memory is bigger — it remembers a user across entirely separate visits, days or weeks apart. The pattern is a per-user memory store keyed by a stable user id: durable facts and preferences are saved under that id and loaded at the start of every new session. Because this data is long-lived and personal, the pattern also demands privacy controls — scoping, consent, and expiry — so memory doesn't become a liability.
nestedConcepts: expiry & the right to be forgotten

subtopics.title: A session ends; the user persists
subtopics.explanation: Within-session memory (the thread's history and checkpoints) is thrown away or archived when the visit ends, but the person comes back tomorrow expecting to be remembered. Cross-session memory is the durable layer that outlives any single thread and is tied to the user, not the conversation. Separating 'this visit' from 'this user' is the conceptual move that makes long-term personalization possible.

subtopics.title: Key the store by a stable user id
subtopics.explanation: Cross-session memory lives in a store addressed by a user id that stays the same across visits — not the thread or session id, which change every time. Everything you know about a user is saved and fetched under that one key. Choosing a stable, per-user key is what lets memory follow the person from one session to the next instead of resetting.

subtopics.title: Load memory when a new session starts
subtopics.explanation: At the beginning of each session you look up the user's memory by id and seed the fresh context with it, so the agent starts already knowing the person. If the user is new, you start empty and begin learning. Front-loading the user's durable facts is the step that turns a cold, generic session into a warm, personalized one from the first message.
subtopics.example:
def start_session(store, user_id: str) -> list[dict]:
    mem = store.get(user_key(user_id))
    system = "You are a helpful assistant."
    if mem and mem.get("facts"):
        known = "; ".join(mem["facts"])
        system += f" Known about the user: {known}."
    return [{"role": "system", "content": system}]
# the very first reply already reflects the user's preferences

subtopics.title: Scope memory to the user and get consent
subtopics.explanation: Because cross-session memory is personal and durable, it must be strictly scoped so one user's facts can never leak into another's context, and it should only store what the user has agreed to remember. Access is gated by the authenticated user id, and sensitive categories are excluded by policy. Treating memory as regulated personal data — scoped and consented — is what separates a helpful feature from a privacy incident.

subtopics.title: Expire memory and support the right to be forgotten
subtopics.explanation: Long-lived memory goes stale and accumulates risk, so each fact carries a time-to-live after which it decays or is dropped, and users must be able to delete everything on demand. Expiry keeps the store fresh and shrinks the blast radius of a leak, while a delete path satisfies regulations like GDPR. Building expiry and erasure in from the start is what keeps long-term memory both accurate and legally defensible.
subtopics.example:
import time

def prune_expired(mem: dict, now=None) -> dict:
    now = now or time.time()
    mem["facts"] = [f for f in mem["facts"] if f["expires_at"] > now]
    return mem

def forget_user(store, user_id: str) -> None:
    store.delete(user_key(user_id))   # right to be forgotten
# stale facts drop out; a delete wipes the whole per-user record

foundations.overview: Within a single visit, persistence and checkpoints let an agent resume a conversation. Cross-session memory is the next layer up: remembering a user across entirely separate sessions, sometimes weeks apart. The pattern is a per-user memory store keyed by a stable user id — not the thread or session id, which change each visit. Durable facts and preferences are written under that user key, and at the start of every new session the agent loads them to seed a fresh context, so it starts already knowing the person. Because this data is long-lived and personal, the pattern is inseparable from privacy: memory must be scoped strictly to the authenticated user so it can't leak across accounts, gated by consent so you only keep what the user agreed to, and equipped with expiry (time-to-live/decay) and a delete path for the right to be forgotten. Get the keying and the privacy controls right and you have durable personalization; get them wrong and you have a data-leak or compliance incident.
foundations.formalDefinition: Cross-session memory is a per-user store of durable facts keyed by a stable user identifier, independent of thread/session ids. On session start the agent loads the user's record and injects it into context; writes append or update facts under the user key. The pattern includes access scoping to the authenticated user, consent gating on what may be stored, and lifecycle controls (expiry/decay and deletion) for privacy and freshness.
foundations.whyItMatters: Users expect an assistant to remember them between visits — their preferences, their context, their prior decisions — without repeating everything each time. But that same durable, personal data is exactly what regulations and users care most about, so the pattern only works if identity scoping, consent, expiry, and deletion are built in. Done right it delivers real personalization; done carelessly it cross-contaminates users or violates privacy law.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of a good hotel that keeps a guest profile: it doesn't remember which specific stay you're on, it remembers you — your room preference, allergies, usual order — and greets you accordingly on any future visit. The profile is keyed to your identity, only staff you authorize can read it, and you can ask them to delete it.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Personal assistants recalling preferences across days, support agents that know a returning customer's history, tutoring apps tracking a learner's long-term progress, and product copilots remembering a user's project setup — all keyed by user id with consent and deletion controls, often layered on top of a vector store for semantic recall.
commonUseCases: Customer support that remembers a user's history and context
Copilots recalling a user's project or environment setup

commonMisconceptions.myth: Cross-session memory is just persistence with a longer timeout.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Persistence resumes one thread; cross-session memory is keyed by the user (not the thread) and outlives every thread, which changes both the key design and the privacy requirements.

commonMisconceptions.myth: You can key memory by whatever id the client or model supplies.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Accepting an id from untrusted input lets one user read another's memory. Always scope to the server-side authenticated identity.

commonMisconceptions.myth: More long-term memory is always better.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Unbounded personal memory goes stale, accumulates contradictions, and increases privacy risk and cost. Expiry, decay, and deletion are part of the pattern, not optional extras.

interactiveExamples.title: Consent gating, expiry, and the right to be forgotten
interactiveExamples.explanation: Extend the per-user store with three privacy controls: only store consented, non-sensitive facts; prune facts past their time-to-live; and support a full delete. This shows the lifecycle that keeps long-term memory both fresh and compliant.

code.code:
import time

STORE = {}
SENSITIVE = {"health", "payment", "government_id"}

def key(uid): return f"user:memory:{uid}"

def remember(uid, text, category, consented, ttl_s, now):
    if not consented or category in SENSITIVE:
        return "refused"  # consent gate + sensitive-category block
    mem = STORE.setdefault(key(uid), {"facts": []})
    mem["facts"].append({"text": text, "expires_at": now + ttl_s})
    return "stored"

def load(uid, now):
    mem = STORE.get(key(uid), {"facts": []})
    fresh = [f for f in mem["facts"] if f["expires_at"] > now]  # expiry
    mem["facts"] = fresh
    return [f["text"] for f in fresh]

def forget(uid):
    STORE.pop(key(uid), None)  # right to be forgotten

t0 = 1000.0
print(remember("u-7", "lab results", "health", True, 999, t0))       # blocked
print(remember("u-7", "prefers metric", "preference", True, 10, t0))  # ok
print(load("u-7", now=t0 + 5))    # still fresh
print(load("u-7", now=t0 + 20))   # expired
forget("u-7")
print(load("u-7", now=t0 + 21))   # wiped
code.caption: The health fact is refused, the preference stores then expires after its TTL, and forget() erases the whole record — consent, expiry, and deletion working together.

checkpoints.prompt: What should cross-session memory be keyed by?
checkpoints.explanation: Thread and session ids change every visit, so keying by them resets memory each time. A stable per-user id lets durable facts follow the person across separate sessions, which is the whole point of cross-session memory.

checkpoints.prompt: This memory loader has a serious privacy flaw. What is it?
options: It should use a database, not a store
It trusts a client-supplied user_id, so any user can read anyone's memory by sending a different id
checkpoints.explanation: Taking user_id from untrusted input lets a caller fetch another user's memory just by changing the id. Memory must be keyed by the server-side authenticated identity so one user's facts can never leak into another's context.

checkpoints.prompt: Why do cross-session memories need expiry and a delete path?
options: To make retrieval slower on purpose
Because unbounded personal memory goes stale, accumulates risk, and regulations require erasure on request
checkpoints.explanation: Long-lived personal data drifts out of date, piles up contradictions, and raises privacy exposure; time-to-live/decay keeps it fresh and small, while a delete path satisfies the right to be forgotten (e.g. GDPR).

theory.question: How does cross-session memory differ from within-session persistence, and how do you structure it?
theory.directAnswer: Persistence resumes a single thread using state keyed by a thread/session id that changes each visit. Cross-session memory remembers the user across separate visits, so it's keyed by a stable user id and outlives every thread. You store durable facts under the user key, load them at the start of each session to seed context, and layer privacy controls — scoping, consent, expiry, deletion — on top.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A per-user store of durable facts, addressed by a stable user identifier independent of any thread or session.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Users expect to be remembered between visits, but thread-scoped state is discarded when a visit ends, so a separate user-scoped layer is needed.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Facts are written under a user key; each new session loads the user's record and injects it into a fresh context, and lifecycle rules (consent, TTL, delete) govern what is kept and for how long.

theory.whyImportant: It's the difference between an assistant that resumes a chat and one that actually knows you across days — while staying compliant with privacy expectations.
theory.realWorldExample: A copilot stores 'user's main repo uses Poetry' under their user id; two weeks later, in a brand-new session, it loads that fact and tailors setup steps without asking again.

followUps.question: Why not key by session id with a long TTL?
followUps.answer: Sessions represent visits, not identity; a new visit gets a new session id, so memory keyed that way still resets. Keying by user id is what persists across visits.

followUps.question: How does this relate to vector memory?
followUps.answer: Cross-session memory is often stored in a vector store per user, so recall within it uses the same similarity retrieval as long-term memory — the difference is the user-scoped key and lifecycle.

theory.question: What privacy and safety controls are essential when an agent remembers users across sessions?
theory.directAnswer: Four: strict identity scoping so memory is keyed by the server-side authenticated user and can never cross accounts; consent gating so you only store what the user agreed to and exclude sensitive categories; expiry/decay so facts have a time-to-live and stale data drops out; and a deletion path so users can erase everything on request. Together they keep long-term memory accurate, minimal, and legally defensible.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: The lifecycle and access controls that govern durable personal memory.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Long-lived personal data is exactly what users and regulations care about; without controls it leaks across users, goes stale, or violates privacy law.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Reads and writes use the authenticated identity only; a consent check and sensitive-category block gate writes; each fact carries an expires_at that pruning enforces; and a forget_user operation deletes the whole per-user record.

theory.whyImportant: It's what separates a helpful personalization feature from a data-leak or compliance incident, and it must be designed in, not bolted on.
theory.realWorldExample: A support assistant refuses to store a customer's health note, expires their shipping preference after 90 days, and honors a delete request by wiping the user key — passing a privacy audit as a result.

followUps.question: Why never accept a user_id from the model or client?
followUps.answer: Untrusted ids let a caller read another user's memory; only the server-side authenticated identity is safe to key on.

followUps.question: How does expiry help beyond privacy?
followUps.answer: It also improves accuracy and cost by dropping stale facts that would otherwise contradict newer ones or bloat retrieval.

scenario.question: During review you find the agent occasionally greets a user with another user's details. How do you diagnose the cross-user leak and prevent it?
scenario.directAnswer: Trace how the memory key is derived: a leak means memory is keyed by something non-isolating (a client-supplied id, a shared/global key, or a reused session). Fix by keying strictly on the server-side authenticated user id, removing any path that accepts an id from model or client input, and adding tests that assert one user can never load another's record. Add expiry and deletion so exposure is bounded.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A confidentiality bug where one user's durable memory reaches another user's context.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: The store was keyed by an untrusted or shared identifier, or authentication wasn't enforced on read, so keys collided or could be spoofed.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Audit every read/write for the key source; replace any client/model-provided id with the authenticated identity; namespace keys per user; and add isolation tests plus logging that records which user id each load used, so future regressions are caught.

scenario.whyImportant: Cross-user memory leakage is a severe privacy failure; the fix (authenticated, isolated keys) is foundational to any per-user memory system.
scenario.realWorldExample: Logs showed loads keyed by a session id that was occasionally reused across users; switching the key to the authenticated user id and adding an isolation test eliminated the leaked greetings.

followUps.question: What test would catch this in CI?
followUps.answer: Write A's memory, authenticate as B, assert B's load returns nothing of A's — an isolation test run on every change.

followUps.question: How do you limit damage if a leak still occurs?
followUps.answer: Minimize what's stored (consent + sensitive-category blocks), set short TTLs so records self-expire, and keep a fast deletion path to purge affected data.

keyTakeaways: Persistence resumes one thread; cross-session memory remembers the user across separate visits and is keyed by a stable user id, not a thread/session id.
Write durable facts under the user key and load them at the start of every new session to seed context, so the agent starts already knowing the person.
Always scope memory to the server-side authenticated identity — never a client- or model-supplied id — so one user's memory can't leak into another's.
Gate what you store on consent and exclude sensitive categories; long-term personal memory is regulated data, not a free-for-all.
Build expiry/decay and a deletion path from the start to keep memory fresh, minimal, and compliant with the right to be forgotten.
